#282. The Best Bed Frames, Tested in Our Own Rooms (2026)

To find the best bed frames, the WIRED Reviews team has put more than 35 to the test over the years. Our top pick is Thuma's Classic Bed, but we've also got options for different budgets and preferences. A good bed frame can improve the look of your room, but it also contributes to sleep hygiene and extends the life of your mattress. I've rounded up the team's favorites below, with prices reflecting queen-size frames where applicable.

Be sure to check out our other sleep guides, including the Best Mattresses, Best Hybrid Mattresses, Best Japanese Joinery Bed Frames, Best Bedsheets, and Best Sleep Gifts for more. And if you don't want to upgrade your frame just yet, check out this advice on how to fix bed frame problems.

Updated November 2026: We've added new bed frames from Castlery and Quince. We've also checked for accuracy throughout.

I've owned the Thuma Classic Bed for five years, and it feels as good as new. You don't need a single tool to assemble this solid wood bed frame. The company uses traditional Japanese joinery techniques, and it took me about 15 minutes to put the whole thing together. That means disassembly and reassembly when I had to move was so easy—there are just two thumb screws at the top and bottom edges of the frame, which you can tighten by hand once everything else is in place.

More surprising is how sturdy it is. I've gone through so many bed frames before the Thuma, and after a year or two, there's usually a broken slat or bent metal rod here and there. Or the slats keep falling down, so you have to do that thing where you pull the mattress over your head as you try to shove them back in place (just me?). The Thuma doesn't creak and never slides around. The foam Pillowboard is an additional expense, but it's comfy. Thuma has since added a wood headboard, which is pricier, but that's what I'll probably upgrade to next, since it completes the look. The only downside is how expensive this whole bed frame is (the price has jumped since I first purchased it), but if it helps, the Thuma is made from repurposed wood, and it's UL GreenGuard Gold Certified, meaning low chemical emissions. —Julian Chokkattu

Thuma made its name with a minimalist wooden bed (our top pick, above) with clean lines and a tool-free assembly process that's no more complex than snapping together Lego bricks. The Signature was launched in February 2025 as the brand's first fully upholstered bed. The Thuma Signature has the same Japanese wood joinery at its heart for easy assembly, but covers the frame in soft Italian felted wool or performance linen for a decidedly more posh experience. I've been testing the wool version for a few months. It took less than five minutes for me to assemble, and it's very solid and dead silent, with no squeaking whatsoever. The plush headboard upholstery is pillow-soft, and my only problem with it is remembering not to just lay my head directly on it. Best of all, when it's time to move, this bed pops apart in just a few minutes without any bolts or screws. —Martin Cizmar

DreamCloud (queen, with bamboo headboard)

I really admire Japanese joinery bed frames, not just because of their minimalistic beauty but also their easy, tool-free setup. Trust me, we don’t want my clumsiness around sharp objects. Not all bed frames that follow this blueprint are of the same caliber, with some being far more stable than others, and the price point usually reflects that. DreamCloud's bamboo Japanese joinery bed frame wasn’t just gorgeous, but outfitted with small details that make a big impact. These include tiny additional rods on each of the boards, located where they are stacked atop each other at the ends. The idea is to keep each of the rails that make up the frame even more secure than just the tension of the overall design. There are included foam blocks if you decide to throw in a headboard, so there's no banging against the wall, either. Plus, I’ll never argue with the price tag, which is very within my budget. —Julia Forbes

I was broker than broke when I got my first apartment more than a decade ago, and this cheap bed frame I bought from Amazon is still being circulated among my younger family members. It's as simple as simple gets, but the steel construction means the frame is durable, and you don't need to add a box spring. The 18-inch model leaves a cavernous space beneath the bed that can accommodate several tote-style storage containers—which could be a blessing or a curse depending on the usual state of your bedroom floor. Just keep in mind that there is no edge whatsoever. This thing is basically a table for your mattress, but it'll get the job done.

I've tested nearly a dozen different bed frames during my time leading this coverage area for the WIRED Reviews team, and the Saatva Siena is probably the prettiest and most elegant I've ever tried. The leather upholstery just makes it feel so grown-up. It's sexy but not straight out of a dark romance dungeon. It's a statement piece that blends in with my decor. I like the free in-room delivery and the rich smell of leather. However, while the frame itself is exceedingly stable, it does slide around on my hardwood floors (I'm planning on attaching some rubbery grips to the feet to remedy this). My main complaint is that you can see the slats of the frame when you're close to the mattress. From a distance, it looks OK, but the white slats are so obvious up close, if you're looking, that it takes away from the whole put-together effect for me. It's also the perfect awkward height to attract dust bunnies that can be difficult to clean unless you move the bed to sweep or vacuum. Overall, these drawbacks are minor, and I still think this frame is worth your consideration. I'll just cross my fingers that none of my Hinge dates look too closely.

When the crib phase ends, this is the bed to get. I upgraded my son from a crib that converted into a toddler bed into this actual kids’ bed, and everyone is sleeping better for it. Nestig originally caught my eye for its adjustable crib, and the Nestig Wave Kids Bed shares similar design elements, with its wooden headboard and side panels. This bed frame can be used as either a Montessori-style floor bed or a standard twin, depending on whether you add the legs. It can accommodate a variety of twin-sized mattresses, and my son loves climbing into his bed each night and demanding I lie down with him while we read. The floor bed aspect is handy since I quietly roll out of the bed and onto the floor to escape his grip, and I like knowing that if my son rolled out of bed, he doesn’t have far to go. When it's time to add the legs, I'll have to take the frame apart partially, which is a small con but not a deal-breaker. —Nena Farrell

Small bedroom? Mobility issues? Don’t want to block a window? You might want to consider a low-profile frame. They’re typically under 11 inches high as opposed to around 20 inches for a traditional frame, which means you may not get as much under-bed storage, but for many, the benefits outweigh this drawback. (The Cooper has about 7 inches of clearance off the floor.) I personally have been grappling with not wanting to block a large window with a headboard, and I was curious if a low-profile frame might be the answer. Sure enough, it was—this 38-inch-tall frame hits just 2 inches below the windowsill and looks fantastic. In fact, the minimalist, mid-century-inspired Cooper is practically indistinguishable from similar frames being sold by Pottery Barn and Crate and Barrel, but runs around $500 less.

With its angled legs and rounded corners, the Cooper definitely has Thuma vibes, but does not feature Japanese joinery construction. It requires some assembly; namely, joining the rails together and screwing down the slats. If you’d rather not deal with this, white-glove delivery is available for $199. For my test unit, it took the delivery driver about 20 minutes to assemble, and in the few months I’ve had it, there haven’t been any squeaks, creaks, or loosening hardware. Note that an 8- to 12-inch mattress is recommended. —Kat Merck

If you prefer the look of fabric covers, the Awara Platform frame will be a good fit. It's simple to assemble, and the pieces are easy to move. The spruce wooden slats are all attached together, so once you have the four frame pieces assembled, simply roll the slats out and they'll attach via hook-and-loop closures to the frame itself. The frame's height is nice, too. It's elevated just enough to make your bed look refined, but not so much that you'll end up losing things underneath your mattress. Though be aware, I did seem to stub my toes on this bed frame more than others I've tested.

This adjustable base is from the makers of one of our favorite mattresses overall and one of our favorite mattresses for side sleepers. It runs on electricity to move the hydraulic-like motors below, which raise both the head and foot area of the bed. It comes with a wireless Bluetooth-enabled remote with buttons to adjust the head and foot portion of the bed up and down, a built-in flashlight, and a button to bring the frame down to a flat level.

The Legget & Platt app can act as a remote as well—a huge sigh of relief for a generally scatterbrained person like myself who's prone to losing things. In the app, you name your bed, make the adjustments, and save your favorite positions so you can easily go back to them. The bed frame is sleek—not bulky at all—and is around 13 inches off the ground, making extra storage space underneath that I didn’t have before. The legs are virtually invisible, although the zero-clearance design allows the base to be used without the legs if using platform bases.

The adjustable frame rises in half-inch increments from 13 to 18 inches from the original base, and the motor is fairly quiet. The base works with mattresses designed to flex, without shifting inside materials or weakening the structure, and is compatible with nearly all Saatva mattresses. For non-Saatva mattresses, check with the manufacturer to ensure it's compatible with an adjustable base.

Saatva provides a 10-year warranty as well as free in-room delivery and setup, and the deliverymen were done in less than 15 minutes, even putting my old mattress back on for me. I often work in my bed and use pillows to prop me up, and this took away the need to be surrounded by a dozen or so of my favorite body pillows. This customizable frame would work great for those with mobility issues or health issues like acid reflux, restless leg syndrome, sleep apnea, or sciatica (among other things). This bougie bed base isn’t completely necessary for me, but it’s a fun luxury to have. —Molly Higgins

This bed frame took me an entire day to build, but it was worth it. It has versions with and without storage, and I chose a storage version to fill the drawers with my various bedding. Adding the storage does nearly double the price and adds to your building time, but the drawers are really useful if it’s something you want. It’s a beautiful bed frame that's felt very stable for the two months I’ve been sleeping on it so far. Even with my questionable building skills, there hasn’t been a squeak when I’m sleeping or getting into bed.

You will want to add on a slatted bed base from Ikea for full support if you don’t have a mattress base already. I really liked pairing this frame with the Lönset slatted bed base for great support on my back. There’s also the cheaper Luröy base if you’re on a budget. —Nena Farrell

I don't say this lightly or often, but I feel like Silk & Snow could charge much more for this Oeko-Tex-certified bed frame. Assembly was annoying—give me video instructions or give me death!—and slightly fiddly, with many individual pieces that you need to screw in or slot together. But the frame is sturdy, the upholstered fabric is soft and durable, and the slats are nice and supportive. The best feature is the built-in storage drawer, which slides out smoothly and closes tightly with magnets. It strikes the perfect balance of form and function.

It doesn't have as much storage space as the lift-up option we recommend from Castlery, but there's room for spare linens, off-season clothing, or certain unmentionables that you don't want lying around out in the open. Be aware that closing the drawer while your bedmate is sleeping will absolutely jolt them awake. But overall, this affordable bed frame offers a good mix of pleasant aesthetics and practical storage solutions.

If your bedroom needs decluttering, the Auburn is a worthwhile investment in your mental well-being. Covered in Castlery’s spill-resistant bouclé fabric, the Auburn proved surprisingly durable against my cats, who treat my furniture like their personal playground. Although I was initially worried about the creamy white—a shade most pet owners might avoid—it's still pristine after a month. Aesthetically, I adore the wingback upholstered headboard and low-profile design. The dense-looped Cambria textile is soft without being overly delicate.

My favorite feature, though, is the lift-up storage compartment, ideal for my 700-ish-square-foot apartment. It’s not tall enough for full-size suitcases, but it accommodates all the random items that typically lack a designated spot—duffels, Christmas ornaments, a cat stroller, etc. Castlery offers white-glove delivery, provided the bedroom is ready. Assembly is doable alone, but it’s easier with two people. —Boutayna Chokrane

Good design is entirely subjective, but I can't get over how pretty this bed frame is. The plush velvet upholstery and padded headboard are stunning and a worthy trade-off if you don't mind the upkeep of cleaning and maintaining upholstered furniture. My tester had to assemble this bed frame herself due to delivery logistics and said it was a massive pain in her nether regions. Typically, this bed comes with white-glove service, where technicians assemble it for you, and she implores you to choose that option if at all possible. The storage is nice and roomy—the bed is being tested by a teenager who likes having extra space to put her ever-growing collections of stuff. The bed is quite sturdy, heavy, and difficult to move, so ensure that any tasks like painting or carpet cleaning are complete, and make sure you know exactly where you want it. For someone looking for an elegant storage bed that will be the centerpiece of their room, this is the perfect option.

This simple, lightweight bed frame from Quince still has a nice aesthetic touch thanks to the removable linen slipcover. The frame itself is easy enough to move around in case of emergency furniture rearranging, and the removable cover can be spot-cleaned as needed. Just be aware that since it's a platform bed, there's absolutely no storage space to speak of. Our teen tester was bummed they couldn't put their slippers under the bed anymore. Otherwise, though, this frame is nice and effective, with sturdy construction and enough available finishes that it could suit any bedroom.

Silk & Snow Wooden Bed Frame: This stunning frame is easy on the eyes with its rich wood finish, though it was delicate and too easy to scuff for our tastes. The legs didn't wobble, the tool-free assembly was easy, and the frame was solid otherwise, but it's too precious for daily use unless you're really careful (or don't mind the wear and tear).

Nest Bedding Woodland Platform Bed: This no-tools-required frame can be put together and taken apart in minutes. The hook-and-latch design lets you piece the frame into a rectangle quickly. Roll out the slats and you're done. The frame feels sturdy and is available in three different finishes, though there are no returns or trials.

KD Frames Nomad Platform Bed: I've put together two Nomad beds from KD Frames, and I know I've got a few more in me. This simple, sturdy bed frame is made in Athens, Georgia, from tulip poplar. Tulip poplar looks like pine, but it's hardwood, and the twin size of this bed can support 600 pounds. The Nomad has clean lines and comes unfinished, meaning you can easily stain it to fit your other furniture. Best of all, it costs about $300 and can be set up in about 20 minutes. —Martin Cizmar

Tempur-ActiveBreeze: I’ll go ahead and rip the bandage off—the only way you can get this adjustable frame and enjoy it to its full potential is if you purchase it with its accompanying smart bed, the Tempur-Pedic Tempur-ActiveBreeze. Stick with me, though, as it’s a cooling bed unlike any I’ve seen before. The base contains fans that can blow hot or cold air at three levels within the mattress to disperse along the surface. It’s pricey, but I didn’t wake up sweating once during testing. —Julia Forbes

Latitude Run Platform Bed Frame: In my quest for finding Thuma dupes, I came across this promising, affordable option on Wayfair. When it first arrived, I wasn’t blown away—the bamboo legs felt too lightweight to adequately hold up heavier mattresses, and tears were shed while assembling the headboard, as it required tools and many, many bolts. The premise of true Japanese joinery frames is that they are tool-free; the headboard didn’t fit the bill here. Once it was up and running, though, it held its own, supporting different mattress types and weights. It didn’t squeak at all, which was shocking. I’m sorry for not having more initial faith in this frame. —Julia Forbes

We used these bed frames exactly like you would. We assembled them ourselves when possible, and we slept on them over the course of weeks, if not months or years. (The minimum time for consideration was one week.) We looked for frames that were durable and worth their cost, taking into account unique features, ease of assembly, and solid construction. Many of these frames are being kept around our homes for long-term durability testing. Frames that aren't kept for long-term testing are donated.

Some brands offer white-glove delivery, where nice folks will come and deliver your bed frame already set up (or, depending on the brand, assemble it in the room of your choice), and then remove the packaging. Sometimes they'll even take your old one (that may come with an upcharge). White-glove delivery is nice, but note that you'll need to make sure the area is completely clear so the delivery people have room to maneuver around.

If you choose to assemble the bed frame yourself, most of the time any tools that are required are included. You might need (or want) to provide your own screwdriver, and you can also expect to use an Allen wrench or a small wrench to tighten down fasteners. Assembly is almost always easier with two people, but it's achievable with one. Be prepared to put out a lot of recycling—there's usually an abundance of cardboard, styrofoam, and other packing material. And if you're pairing your new frame with a new mattress, we have tips on assembly for those, too.

Do You Need a Bed Frame, Headboard, Footboard, or Box Spring?

Technically, you could plop your mattress on the floor and call it a day. But experts recommend using a bed frame for many reasons. Bed frames support your mattress, which in turn helps the mattress last longer by ensuring even weight distribution and preventing issues like sagging. That added support can help with your sleep quality, too. And they provide circulation under your mattress, which helps eliminate any odors, disperse any heat, and prevent moisture buildup. Finally, bed frames usually provide under-bed storage—and where else are you going to put your seasonal clothes or luggage?

Box springs are hit or miss. Most bed frames nowadays have a solid enough foundation that you don't need to provide a box spring. WIRED's in-house mattress expert, Julia Forbes, has an article where she breaks down exactly when one might be necessary. But if your mattress is made out of certain materials like memory foam with no inner support structure, or your bed frame doesn't have slats to support your mattress, a box spring might be smart. Check with your mattress manufacturer for specific recommendations.

Headboards are purely for aesthetics. You don't need one unless you really want to protect your walls from scuffs, or if you want a place to lean against while you're chilling in bed.

#280. Microsoft's historic cloud outage exposed an engineering “fog of war”

Internal memos reveal a “Code Red” overhaul and ambitious one-hour recovery goals.

According to internal memos reviewed by Reuters, Microsoft has declared a “Code Red” overhaul of its engineering response practices after the November 12 outage that lost access to Exchange Online, Teams, and Outlook for users worldwide.

Per the memos, Microsoft 365 Core President Jason Henderson described the outage as having the most customer impact in the history of Exchange Online. In a separate memo, Henderson wrote that an urgent production fix in a recent incident took five to six days to reach worldwide saturation. Microsoft’s target for its most urgent security fixes is to move from detection to safe worldwide deployment in one hour. “Needless to say, we aren’t here yet,” Henderson wrote.

The memos, which Reuters reviewed but Microsoft has not published, outline the response to the November 12 disruption. The company’s post-incident report, dated November 20, attributed the downtime to an undetected Windows scalability defect introduced in July, which caused lock contention in the gateway processes. A Teams traffic failover then dumped additional load onto infrastructure already under stress, as maintenance had left nearly 14 percent of gateway server capacity offline at the time of the incident.

Amanda Silver, a corporate vice president overseeing Microsoft 365 Core and Work IQ, wrote that engineers had to contend with a “fog of war” as the outage unfolded. According to Silver, responders exchanged more than 11,000 messages across 11 Teams chats, leaving diagnostic data scattered, and a full view of the incident fractured. Silver’s memo also quotes Charles Lamanna, executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, telling a Code Red review that the affected component had accumulated “roughly ten years’ worth of acceptable failures.”

Microsoft has said the outage was not related to any cyberattack or malicious activity, and the defects were not caused by AI tooling. As part of the Code Red overhaul, Silver’s memo outlines five workstreams focused on load shedding, geographic traffic partitioning, and faster recovery mechanisms. According to Reuters, Microsoft plans to improve its incident response and patching timelines by deploying its own AI agents to help engineers diagnose system health data more quickly. Henderson said that he will hold daily meetings with the Substrate leadership team, which oversees the engineering team responsible for Microsoft 365 services.

Microsoft has set targets of a one-hour worldwide resolution in major incidents and a one-hour deployment window for urgent security fixes. It hasn’t said when it hopes to meet them or how future response efforts will avoid 11 separate Teams chats and the “fog of war.”

#279. Anthropics Claude now lets you turn artifacts into apps

So you asked Claude to help you remember when to take out the trash, and it ridiculously over-engineered it and created a beautiful interactive artifact with timelines, graphs, and a calendar? Well, now that you've gotten that far, why not turn the artifact into a full-fledged app on your desktop?

A new update to Anthropic's Claude allows you to do exactly that, though there are some limitations.

Artifacts, if you aren't familiar with Claude, are work outputs that are similar to webpages, and they can contain charts, graphs, text, photos, videos, and interactive elements, but until now they only lived inside Claude. Now, when you open an artifact in Claude, you can click on the drop-down menu on the top left and select "Install as an app."

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

Besides being more convenient, since they live on your desktop, these apps can perform actions such as sending notifications or adding items to your menu bar. Of course, you can set permissions for apps to make sure they don't overstep their boundaries; by default, they can only do what they'd be able to do in a browser, but you can go as far as to give them full access to your computer.

I've tried this out on my Mac, and it worked well, though I couldn't install all my artifacts as apps. Anthropic says some artifacts can't be installed as apps, which includes Claude Docs, Slides, and Sheets.

The ability to install artifacts as apps is rolling out to all plans as a beta feature. It's on by default for Team plans; on Enterprise, it's off until an owner turns it on.

#277. How Do Cooking Pros Decide the ‘Best’ Recipe for Something?

Back in my malleable twenties, I had a big phase with John Coltrane's version of “My Favorite Things.” It was a deep enough crush that it got me thinking about what my own favorite things were, and what made them favorites.

It was a nice thing to talk about with people, and of course, my list always had a bunch of kitchen gear and cookbooks on it. It's not too hard to draw a line from that time to becoming a food writer and kitchen gear reviewer. Finding the best and figuring out what makes it great became a career-defining quest.

Incredibly important on this path was finding (or maybe stealing?) my mom's copy of The Best Recipe cookbook from Cook's Illustrated, one of the charmingly nerdier wings of America's Test Kitchen. That book applied the scientific method to recipes to create "best" versions, documenting their dead ends and successes en route to the perfect flan, mashed potatoes, or boiled green beans. As they put it right on the cover, "Would you make 38 versions of crème caramel to find the absolute best version? We did."

When I worked as a line cook, I always wondered about the food I was making: Why this combination of ingredients? Why that technique? Here was a book that answered those questions while bolstering my kitchen foundations.

When it came out in 1999, the internet wasn't yet where you went for dinnertime inspiration, meaning you'd find a recipe in a cookbook or magazine or newspaper, or dig around in the recipe box. Now, you can spend hours researching different “best” methods to make a recipe, wondering if you'll know perfect when you see it.

“It's a trap to think like that,” says Ella Quittner, a culture and food writer, and author of the new cookbook Obsessed With the Best, a spiritual descendant of Best Recipe. “Perfect food doesn't exist. For an individual, it exists for the moment and a place in time.”

Perfect on a leisurely Saturday afternoon is very different from perfect on a busy Tuesday evening at 6 pm.

But it's different when Quittner is coming up with a recipe.

“I do a huge amount of research through cookbooks, magazines, websites, cookbooks from the 18th century, or something from TikTok last week,” she says. “I'll take my findings and try to braid them together. I don't want a Frankenstein dish. I want deep flavor, not too fussy. It should seem like the right amount of labor for the result you're seeking.”

On the simpler side, she boldly updates Marcella Hazan's famous tomato sauce. Quittner admiringly explains how in Hazan's seemingly simple tomato-butter-onion-salt version, it uses an onion “to flavor the sauce like it would in a stock.” It also teaches “the power of simmering an acidic ingredient with a fat ingredient over low heat over time.” She calls it a fundamental flavor-building technique where “the fat rounds out the acid and the acid helps taste the fat.” Or, as she says, “acid lifts, fat deepens.” For her update, she quarters the onions and caramelizes their flat surfaces in butter, adding depth and sweetness. Building on something her parents did when she was a kid, she lays down a dab of ricotta before the sauce-coated noodles go in the bowl, a luxurious pasta trick I am adding to my forever repertoire.

At America's Test Kitchen, they go to similar lengths, but on a comparatively industrial scale, using what chief content officer Dan Souza refers to as a “crystal-clear process with specific goals.”

They dive into their “massive” cookbook library, look at what's online, then pull five representative recipes from that research, weaving them together with their own expertise to create a working recipe. “Typically, that's fine, and then we iterate,” Souza says. From there, up to 25 staff members might contribute to the recipe, a process that can take six weeks before it is sent to a subset of their army of—get this—75,000 volunteer recipe testers.

“They can change what we do,” Souza says. “It helps make the recipe bulletproof.”

“When I was a kid, my mom used to make pizza on a sheet pan, and it had lots of cheese on it. It was a pizza, and I loved it,” he says. “Now she's got a baking steel, and her pizza is at a completely different level.”

Sometimes, to get to that level, or simply get the hang of something new, the language in the recipe or headnote needs to get you there.

“Sometimes people write casual, chatty, recipes. Sometimes it's like a list,” says Sarah Billingsley, food and lifestyle publishing director for Chronicle Books.

She loves it when she finds an author who has cooked something so many times that they have “a casual and unique way to describe a step.” Instead of “cook until browned,” it might be “cook until the edges of the leeks start to frazzle.”

As we talk, we get into a mutual appreciation of Ukrainian author Anna Voloshyna and her cookbooks. Billingsley draws my attention to the descriptions in the baked milk recipe in Voloshyna's new book, Ukraïne, where you learn that young chefs in Ukraine are popularizing a classic recipe, baking milk and nothing more in a Dutch oven for 8 to 10 hours and using it in desserts, coffee, and to make fresh cheeses.

Since few stateside readers will have made it or encountered the dense brown skin that forms on its surface, Voloshyna offers near-poetic counsel: “Don't break the skin until after the milk is out of the oven and has cooled. You will know the milk is ready when it smells nutty and the skin on top is a deep golden brown.”

Regardless of how you write a recipe, you need to know what a perfect version of a dish tastes like in the first place. That's on full display in chef Pim Techamuanvivit and coauthor Andrea Nguyen's new book, Cooking Thai.

Techamuanvivit has earned Michelin stars for her restaurants in Bangkok and San Francisco, and Nguyen has written several award-winning Vietnamese cookbooks. Together, Nguyen says, they strove to “get the reader to Pim's palate” even if that reader doesn't have a perfect understanding of the cuisine.

To do this, sometimes you need a power combo like these two to act as what Nguyen calls a chief arbiter of taste.

“You need someone to tell you this is what's good,” and as she said this, I imagined her handing me a small bowl of the pork and sour leaf curry on page 176. “Pim was raised in that culture, and she'll tell you she's a home cook, but she knows the technique. She is the perfect person to create a cookbook that will be around for years.”

To help get their readers there, Nguyen points out how the book has a front section with photos of the exact ingredients called for, like an image of earthy, medicinal galangal with the gentle plea: “Please do not substitute ginger,” and a photo of Golden Mountain Seasoning Sauce that a shopper could look for online or at the market. You can play around once you get the hang of things, but until then, listen to the experts and spring for the Golden Mountain. Do not substitute ginger for galangal.

“Pim and I, we're in our mid-life. We've been around. Good food doesn't need to be elevated. It's already perfect,” she says. “A recipe is like driving instructions. Sometimes you take a detour. A perfect recipe has guardrails to help you complete and succeed and reach your destination.”

#275. The haunting Masters meltdown that changed Rory McIlroy's career

Editor’s Note:  This story was originally published in April 2023.

Slumped on his club, head buried in his arm, Rory McIlroy looked on the verge of tears.

The then-21-year-old had just watched his ball sink into the waters of Rae’s Creek at Augusta National and with it, his dream of winning The Masters, a dream that had looked so tantalizingly close mere hours earlier.

As a four-time major winner and one of the most decorated names in the sport’s history, few players would turn down the chance to swap places with McIlroy heading into Augusta this week.

Yet on Sunday afternoon of April 10, 2011, not a golfer in the world would have wished to be in the Northern Irishman’s shoes.

A fresh-faced, mop-headed McIlroy had touched down in Georgia for the first major of the season with a reputation as the leading light of the next generation of stars.

An excellent 2010 had marked his best season since turning pro three years earlier, highlighted by a first PGA Tour win at the Quail Hollow Championship and a crucial contribution to Team Europe’s triumph at the Ryder Cup.

Yet despite a pair of impressive top-three finishes at the Open and PGA Championship respectively, a disappointing missed cut at The Masters – his first at a major – served as ominous foreshadowing.

McIlroy shot 74 and 77 to fall four strokes short of the cut line at seven-over par, a performance that concerned him enough to take a brief sabbatical from competition.

But one year on in 2011, any lingering Masters demons looked to have been exorcised as McIlroy flew round the Augusta fairways.

Having opened with a bogey-free seven-under 65 – the first time he had ever shot in the 60s at the major – McIlroy pulled ahead from Spanish first round co-leader Alvaro Quirós with a second round 69.

It sent him into the weekend holding a two-shot cushion over Australia’s Jason Day, with Tiger Woods a further stroke behind and back in the hunt for a 15th major after a surging second round 66.

And yet the 21-year-old leader looked perfectly at ease with having a target on his back. Even after a tentative start to the third round, McIlroy rallied with three birdies across the closing six holes to stretch his lead to four strokes heading into Sunday.

The youngster was out on his own ahead of a bunched chasing pack comprising Day, Ángel Cabrera, K.J. Choi and Charl Schwartzel. After 54 holes, McIlroy had shot just three bogeys.

“It’s a great position to be in … I’m finally feeling comfortable on this golf course,” McIlroy told reporters.

“I’m not getting ahead of myself, I know how leads can dwindle away very quickly. I have to go out there, not take anything for granted and go out and play as hard as I’ve played the last three days. If I can do that, hopefully things will go my way.

“We’ll see what happens tomorrow because four shots on this golf course isn’t that much.”

The truth can hurt, and McIlroy was about to prove his assessment of Augusta to be true in the most excruciating way imaginable.

His fourth bogey of the week arrived immediately. Having admitted to expecting some nerves at the first tee, McIlroy sparked a booming opening drive down the fairway, only to miss his putt from five feet.

Three consecutive pars steadied the ship, but Schwartzel had the wind in his sails. A blistering birdie, par, eagle start had seen him draw level at the summit after his third hole.

A subsequent bogey from the South African slowed his charge, as McIlroy clung onto a one-shot lead at the turn from Schwartzel, Cabrera, Choi, and a rampaging Woods, who shot five birdies and an eagle across the front nine to send Augusta into a frenzy.

Despite his dwindling advantage and the raucous Tiger-mania din ahead of him, McIlroy had responded well to another bogey at the 5th hole, draining a brilliant 20-foot putt at the 7th to restore his lead.

The fist pump that followed marked the high-water point of McIlroy’s round, as a sliding start accelerated into full-blown free-fall at the par-four 10th hole.

His tee shot went careening into a tree, ricocheting to settle between the white cabins that separate the main course from the adjacent par-three course. It offered viewers a glimpse at a part of Augusta rarely seen on broadcast, followed by pictures of McIlroy anxiously peering out from behind a tree to track his follow-up shot.

Though his initial escape was successful, yet another collision with a tree and a two-putt on the green saw a stunned McIlroy eventually tap in for a triple bogey. Having led the field one hole and seven shots earlier, he arrived at the 11th tee in seventh.

By the time his tee drive at the 13th plopped into the creek, all thoughts of who might be the recipient of the green jacket had long-since switched away from the anguished youngster. It had taken him seven putts to navigate the previous two greens, as a bogey and a double bogey dropped him to five-under – the score he had held after just 11 holes of the tournament.

Mercifully, the last five holes passed without major incident. A missed putt for birdie from five feet at the final hole summed up McIlroy’s day, though he was given a rousing reception as he left the green.

Mere minutes earlier, the same crowd had erupted as Schwartzel sunk his fourth consecutive birdie to seal his first major title. After starting the day four shots adrift of McIlroy, the South African finished 10 shots ahead of him, and two ahead of second-placed Australian duo Jason Day and Adam Scott.

McIlroy’s eight-over 80 marked the highest score of the round. Having headlined the leaderboard for most of the week, he finished tied-15th.

Tears would flow during a phone call with his parents the following morning, but at his press conference, McIlroy was upbeat.

“I’m very disappointed at the minute, and I’m sure I will be for the next few days, but I’ll get over it,” he said.

“I was leading this golf tournament with nine holes to go, and I just unraveled … It’s a Sunday at a major, what it can do.

“This is my first experience at it, and hopefully the next time I’m in this position I’ll be able to handle it a little better. I didn’t handle it particularly well today obviously, but it was a character-building day … I’ll come out stronger for it.”

Once again, McIlroy would be proven right.

Just eight weeks later in June, McIlroy rampaged to an eight-shot victory at the US Open. Records tumbled in his wake at Congressional, as he shot a tournament record 16-under 268 to become the youngest major winner since Tiger Woods at The Masters in 1997.

The historic victory kickstarted a golden era for McIlroy. After coasting to another eight-shot win at the PGA Championship in 2012, McIlroy became only the third golfer since 1934 to win three majors by the age of 25 with triumph at the 2014 Open Championship.

Before the year was out, he would add his fourth major title with another PGA Championship win.

And much of it was owed to that fateful afternoon at Augusta. In an interview with the BBC in 2015, McIlroy dubbed it “the most important day” of his career.

“If I had not had the whole unravelling, if I had just made a couple of bogeys coming down the stretch and lost by one, I would not have learned as much.

“Luckily, it did not take me long to get into a position like that again when I was leading a major and I was able to get over the line quite comfortably. It was a huge learning curve for me and I needed it, and thankfully I have been able to move on to bigger and better things.

“Looking back on what happened in 2011, it doesn’t seem as bad when you have four majors on your mantelpiece.”

McIlroy’s contentment came with a caveat: it would be “unthinkable” if he did not win The Masters in his career.

Yet as he prepares for his 15th appearance at Augusta National this week, a green jacket remains an elusive missing item from his wardrobe.

Despite seven top-10 finishes in his past 10 Masters outings, the trophy remains the only thing separating McIlroy from joining the ranks of golf immortals to have completed golf’s career grand slam of all four majors in the modern era: Gene Sarazen, Ben Hogan, Gary Player, Jack Nicklaus, and Tiger Woods.

A runner-up finish to Scottie Scheffler last year marked McIlroy’s best finish at Augusta, yet arguably 2011 remains the closest he has ever been to victory. A slow start in 2022 meant McIlroy had begun Sunday’s deciding round 10 shots adrift of the American, who teed off for his final hole with a five-shot lead despite McIlroy’s brilliant 64 finish.

At 33 years old, time is still on his side. Though 2022 extended his major drought to eight years, it featured arguably his best golf since that golden season in 2014.

And as McIlroy knows better than most, things can change quickly at Augusta National.

#274. Target is giving away free gift cards worth up to $1,000 on Black Friday: How to claim

TL;DR: On Black Friday (Nov. 27), the first 100 guests in line at every Target store get a free $25, $50, or $100 Target gift card — plus one $1,000 winner per store (no purchase necessary).

Target is giving early birds a major incentive to set their alarms on Black Friday morning. On Friday, Nov. 27, the retailer is handing out free Target gift cards worth $25, $50, or $100 to the first 100 eligible guests in line at every store — plus one lucky shopper at each location will walk away with a $1,000 Target gift card.

Unlike online doorbusters that disappear in seconds, this giveaway happens strictly in person and comes with a tight arrival and redemption window.

Target stores reopen at 6 a.m. local time on Black Friday, Nov. 27. Showing up right at 6 a.m. will be too late if you want a free gift card. Target associates will start handing out prize redemption tickets to the first 100 eligible people in line roughly an hour before doors open (around 5 a.m. local time at most stores).

Tickets are handed out on a first-come, first-served basis while supplies last, with a strict limit of one ticket per person.

Once doors open at 6 a.m. local time, you have to take your ticket to the Black Friday event cart inside that same Target store within one hour of store opening (by 7 a.m. local time at 6 a.m. locations). If you miss that one-hour redemption window, you forfeit your prize.

Your card's exact dollar value is revealed when you redeem your ticket at the event cart. Out of the 100 winners at every store, 60 people get a $25 gift card, 30 get a $50 gift card, nine get a $100 gift card, and one person gets the $1,000 grand prize.

The giveaway is open to shoppers ages 13 and older (minors need a parent or legal guardian's permission to participate), and no purchase is necessary to get a ticket or claim a card.

Once you claim your gift card, you can spend it right away on Target's Black Friday sale or save it for later in stores and online — just note that you cannot use it on prepaid or specialty gift cards. Anything you buy that's eligible also qualifies for Target's Holiday Price Match Guarantee through Dec. 24.

Double-check your local Target's exact hours before heading out — and if you are mapping out a multi-store morning route, check out our guide to Black Friday 2026 store hours to see when other major retailers open their doors.

Soumya is a deals writer who covers consumer tech, shopping deals, and the products people use every day. With experience writing about everything from AI tools and software to smartphones and home gadgets, she enjoys breaking down product research into clear, useful recommendations. When she's not tracking deals, she's usually comparing products, digging through reviews, and figuring out what actually makes a purchase worth it.

#273. Best Robot Vacuum of 2026: Shark, Eufy, Roborock

I've recently introduced a few friends to the power of a great robot vacuum. One of my friends calls hers a marriage saver, while the other was both thrilled and horrified by how many stains the vacuum’s AI found on her floors. Personally, my robot vacuums keep me from wanting to set the litter box on fire, since my cat is on a mission to create his own navigational trail of litter through my home.

The best robot vacuums these days aren’t just vacuuming your floors, nor are they blindly bumping around your house like they used to. These gadgets are mopping, scrubbing away stains, lifting themselves off obstacles, and even reminding you to clean the dirtier areas in your home more frequently. A good robot vacuum can cost a pretty penny, but it doesn’t have to, depending on what you’re looking for. Which is the best model for you? I’ve been testing every new robot vacuum I can in my three-story home filled with three adults, a preschooler, and a cat.

Here are the best robot vacuum cleaners I’ve tried this year, and everything we really liked from recent years. Looking for more vacuum ideas? Don't miss our guides to the Best Dyson Vacuums, Best Cordless Vacuums, Best Vacuums for Pet Hair, Best Carpet Cleaners, and Best Vacuums.

Updated November 2026: The Roborock Qrevo 2 Pro is now this guide's budget pick, with the Eufy Omni C28 as a budget runner-up. I've also added the Roborock Saros 20 Flow to Honorable Mentions, and testing notes on the Dyson Nurovi R3, Tapo RV50 Pro Omni, and three iRobot Roomba models (Max 875, Plus 678, and Plus 575). I've also ensured up-to-date links and prices.

I’ve been testing the latest models from our favorite cleaning brands. Here are the top three I’d buy right now.

I was surprised how much I liked the AI-powered Shark PowerDetect UV Reveal. Its UV light revealed spots on my floor where I know I previously had spills, and its built-in AI had the vacuum go back over to deep-clean those spots in a way I clearly hadn’t done before. The UV Reveal also did a great job on my hard floors (both LVP and tile) as a mop-and-vacuum combo, as well as on my builder-grade carpet and a large rug in the living room. I was impressed that the rug actually felt just as fluffy and well-vacuumed as if I had cracked out my favorite Dyson stick vacuum instead of just sending a robot vacuum to do the work for me.

It has an extendable arm, which did a good job passing my corner test. I stuck three Cheerios in tricky corners of my home, and it got two out of three, doing better than the latest Dyson vacuum. It managed to get the trickier two corners too; it skipped the third Cheerio to avoid bumping my bar stools. I also did a spill test with two spots of cherry juice in my home. It mopped away the first spill with no problem, but I did have to send it back out to finish cleaning the second spill. The UV Reveal did great with obstacle avoidance and has “NeverStuck Technology” to lift itself off obstacles, and it worked to get itself off the flat, long legs of one of my side tables. The vacuum finished a cleaning run in a good amount of time, cleaning my entire main floor in about 60 minutes, but it does go back out to scrub all the spots it sees on the floor. That took another 30 minutes for me, but I assume that would get shorter over time, the longer you live with this vacuum and have it cleaning up. Still, 93 minutes to run through four rooms and go back to do some scrub work is a solid time window.

Overall, this vacuum really shines on hard floors, but I also liked it on rugs and carpet if you have a mix of these in your home. It has an auto-empty base with a bagless debris system, so you won’t need to worry about purchasing debris bags to empty the docking station. The only downside is that the vacuum can learn only a single map, so it doesn’t work for multiple floors of your home unless you’re game for it to remap every time (which takes only a couple minutes, so it’s not a horrible experience, but the vacuum will also want the base station lugged up or down the stairs too). The suction is also a mystery; Shark has declined to comment on the exact suction. Still, we’ve loved low-suction vacuums before, and the results have been great.

This vacuum is one I refuse to part with, and while its retail price is technically $800, it's on sale enough in the $500 range that this has become the budget pick I'd easily recommend when it's on sale. The Roborock Qrevo 2 Pro is the newest update to Roborock's more affordable Qrevo line, which went without updates for years. The Qrevo 2 Pro is cheaper than the Curv 2 that launched in January 2026, and it still packs a ton of power, great navigation, and the same handy app. It comes with 20,000 Pa of suction, a FlexiArm mop that does a better job of corner cleaning, and a reversible side brush to help dislodge corner debris. I love seeing the arm reach out and get all the edges and corners around my house, especially underneath cabinets in the kitchen and bathroom.

The Qrevo 2 Pro also pulled ahead in some areas when compared against the similarly often-on-sale Eufy Omni C28. While the Eufy got itself stuck on cords in my bedroom, the Qrevo 2 Pro only attempted to eat cords without actually getting stuck on them. The Qrevo still isn't great at seeing small objects; it took my cat's toys for rides around the room, but they usually didn't get stuck or stop the vacuum. Both vacuums scored a 2 out of 3 on my Cheerio test, but the Qrevo 2 Pro got the harder fridge Cheerio with its FlexiArm mop. The Eufy did a little better on mopping, but neither vacuum did perfectly. I'm giving the Qrevo 2 Pro a 1.25 out of 2—one spill was just about gone, but the area around it was all slightly sticky, while the second spill was only half cleaned. It's hard to grade perfectly. It also occasionally leaves a little debris behind when it goes over thresholds that separate carpet from hard flooring, but it didn't have this issue when transitioning onto rugs.

This vacuum (and its base station) also looks good and is fairly quiet. (Except when it cleans on tile, which is a noisy experience as it travels across the grout divots. But it does a good job.) Both the base station and vacuum itself are quieter than the Eufy Omni C28, and it is especially pleasant if you let the Qrevo 2 Pro vacuum and mop separately. It takes longer than doing the combo cleans, but this vacuum pulled off doing both a separate vacuuming session and mopping of my massive first floor in two hours, which most vacuums still take for combo cleans.

We've loved the app and navigation from Roborock for years, and it still stands out among its rivals in this area. The Roborock only struggles to navigate on a C-shaped table with long, thin, flat legs it can't see against my wood floors. Besides that it does a fantastic job navigating around all kinds of furniture and never runs into anything the way I've seen more expensive vacuums do. It can map multiple floors of my house too. Ultimately, it's a great, well-rounded vacuum for the price.

If the Roborock Qrevo isn't on sale, this Eufy is the next best thing. Former WIRED editor Adrienne So previously recommended Eufy’s older X10 Pro Omni as a great robot vacuum without spending too much, and Eufy released the Eufy Omni C28 in February this year with a similar set of features and price point. The Omni C28 comes with nearly double the suction power of the older model, a self-cleaning roller mop instead of mop pads, and retractable detangling brushes.

It does a solid job mopping and vacuuming, but it has a shorter battery life, leaving it at only 37 percent after completing the four-room main floor of my house. This is a bit of a bummer, since this affordable vacuum can do multi-floor mapping. While it can store enough maps to clean all three levels of my home, it doesn’t have the battery life to do so. But it does charge fairly quickly, and I was able to still clean all three floors of my house in a single day—I just had to let it recharge a little at the base first. It went back up to 57 percent battery life after just 20 minutes in its docking station. It also tried to eat the cords near my bed, and luckily I was nearby to yank them free. If you get this vacuum, make sure your cords are clear of the vacuum's reach.

With my corner Cheerio test, this vacuum also got two out of three Cheerios, but it missed the trickier fridge-corner Cheerio. This is the hardest spot to get into, so I’m not surprised, but it does mean you’ll have to check those corners more with this vacuum. The cherry juice spill test also showed similar results: The first spot it reached was cleaned completely, while the second spot, which had more time to dry, still had some sticky residue left behind.

Overall, though, it’s a good vacuum for the price, especially since it packs multi-floor mapping, the capability to mop and vacuum, and good results all around for a vacuum that’s already usually on sale for around or under $500.

There are a lot of great robot vacuums out there. Here are a few others we’ve tried and liked.

Dreame L60 Ultra for $1,000: This vacuum did a good all-around job and packs a ton of good features, including dual flex arms, the EasyLeap System that lets it move over almost-2-inch tall obstacles, and 35,000 Pa of suction. This is a great one to buy if you have tall thresholds in your home thanks to that lifting feature, but otherwise, you could get a smarter vacuum for a cheaper price. This vacuum does promise dirt detection, but I never noticed it delivering on that promise. Still, my Dreame long-term tester commented that it's leagues quieter than her older Dreame vacuum, so it's a good upgrade choice if you like Dreame and want something quieter.

Dreame X50 Ultra for $800: If you have pets that tend to make one area of your home particularly hair- or debris-covered, this is the vacuum to get. The Dreame X50 Ultra has tons of great features, including double-roll brushes, side wands for edge cleaning, and a large-capacity docking station, but the real standout is the AI that can notice extremely dirty areas. It’s the most effective dirt- and obstacle-identification system that former WIRED editor Adrienne So has tried, and it will even remind her which areas it needs to clean more often (for her, that’s near her dog’s bed).

Dyson Spot+Scrub Ai for $800: The Dyson Spot+Scrub Ai is a good robot vacuum overall, with a unique base station design that calls back to the Dyson stick vacuums and built-in AI to find spots and stains on your floor to scrub them away. It mostly worked, but I did prefer this feature in the Shark above, which has a similar starting retail price but is usually on sale. It’s also a little tall, so if you have builder-grade cabinets like I do, it might not be able to vacuum the toe kicks or underneath your Ikea furniture. (It got stuck underneath my Tolstad bed frame and was too tall to get underneath my Besta cabinet.)

Matic Robot Vacuum Bundle for $1,495: According to former WIRED editor Adrienne So, this vacuum is spectacular. It’s the only 10/10 rating she’s ever given a robot vacuum. Its six RGB infrared cameras do a great job making a 3D map, the single waste bag contains wet and dry debris, it does a great job cleaning toe kicks, and it was quiet enough to run without bothering So’s kids while they watched TV. That’s due to Matic’s lower suction power (only 3,200 Pa), but she didn’t notice any decrease in cleanliness as a result. It’s compact and square, giving it the ability to really get into corners. The only bummer is that it has expensive, proprietary waste bags. But those waste bags do have diaper salts, charcoal, and a HEPA filter, so you don’t have to replace the filters separately.

Narwal Flow for $849: WIRED’s Reviews team hasn’t always had success with Narwal’s vacuums, but when I tested this model late last year, I found it super easy to set up and get cleaning. I had no connectivity issues, installation was a breeze, and the app was easy to navigate. It did a good job cleaning my hard floors and rug, and even when I ran it right out of the box until it ran out of battery, it returned itself to its station to recharge and then resumed the task a few hours later, all on its own. The base station is also sleek and cute compared with the dark, bulky structures most have.

Roborock Saros 20 Flow for $1,300: If you're looking for something with serious suction, the Saros 20 Flow is my preferred choice out of Roborock's higher-power Saros line. I really like using it, and the roller mop does a good job mopping, but it only got one out of three Cheerios on my corner test and didn't manage to spot any stains on my floor, even with the promised built-in stain detection. It's the option I'd choose if you want a robot vacuum with great navigation and super-high suction (36,000 Pa) that won't deposit debris around the house like the Saros 20 tended to, but I think you'd be just as happy with a cheaper Roborock.

Roborock Qrevo Curv 2 for $1,000: This is another great option from Roborock and another part of the Qrevo line we've liked for years. The Qrevo Curv 2 came out in January and has similar strengths to the Qrevo 2 Pro above, but it has a roller mop called SpiraFlow instead of two individual mop pads. It also has similar struggles, with threshold debris and small objects being hard to spot. It's a good vacuum overall, and best on sale (which it often is!), but I'd pick my picks on sale over it.

A robot vacuum is an automated vacuum, usually shaped like a round disc, that moves around your house to vacuum (and mop, as many models these days include mopping) on your behalf. You might’ve heard some refer to these devices as “Roombas,” which is the brand that made the concept popular, but today just about every cleaning brand—from high-end Dyson to affordable Bissell—makes some kind of robot vacuum. They come with either a charging station or a larger docking station that can self-empty.

There are a few things most robot vacuums will need to work properly:

The Federal Communications Commission announced in late July that foreign-produced advanced robotic devices will now be included on the FCC’s Covered List. That list includes communications equipment and services that are deemed to pose an unacceptable risk to the national security of the United States—including robot vacuums (and similar devices like robotic pool cleaners and lawn mowers). While it won’t ban any models already on the market that have FCC approval, we’ll likely see a huge decline in available new models after this year. Models made in the US will be fine, but future vacuums from popular brands like Dreame, Eufy, Roborock, and more could be affected. For now, you'll still see vacuums launching from these brands, though, since FCC approval is given months ahead of product launches.

This decision comes from an interagency body in the White House executive branch called the National Security Determination, which has deemed automated robotic devices a security risk due to the data they collect, which could be used for surveillance and be remotely commandeered by “malign actors.” While the initial documentation describes humanoid robots and a recent case of a humanoid robot’s cybersecurity vulnerability to be remotely taken over, the official description of these robot devices will include robot vacuums and any devices meeting the following criteria:

Overall, robot vacuums themselves aren’t banned, but new models from companies based outside the US won’t get FCC approval and can’t be sold in the US. You don’t need to stop using any robot vacuum you have, but if you’re in the market for a new one, it’s better to shop sooner before availability starts to decline—and prices are likely to rise as supply falls.

Dyson R3 Nurovi Spot+Scrub UV for $1,200: Dyson's newest version of the Spot+Scrub has a UV light to help its AI spot stains, and I was happy to see those stains reported in the app, but I couldn't tell if the vacuum actually did more detailed cleaning in those areas. That aside, I wanted to love this vacuum more than I did. My issue with the vacuum is how it did in regular cleaning sessions: It left pieces of popcorn behind when vacuuming on my downstairs rugs, didn't seem to ever get close enough to my walls for any kind of edge cleaning, and was too tall to get underneath cabinets or basic Ikea furniture around my house (but still smacked into that furniture over and over again due to camera placement). It also got a zero on my corner Cheerio test, failing to even get the Cheerio that just sits near a chair leg. I haven't tested either of the cheaper new Dyson robot vacuum options, but if this is how the best one does, I'm not inclined to.

Eufy S2 for $950: This robot vacuum has an intense-looking base station. However, I was disappointed it missed both the fridge and bookshelf Cheerios in my corner test, giving it only a one out of three. Both cherry stains were scrubbed away, but the floor near where the stains were felt sticky all over even with the stains ostensibly wiped away. It’s especially a bummer given the price point; it needed to do better to be worth such a high price tag.

iRobot Roomba Max 705 Combo for $800: The name Roomba is synonymous with robot vacuums for many people, but it’s actually a specific line made by iRobot. I really liked both the high-end look of the Max 705 Combo (not to be confused with the cheaper Max 705) and the overall job it did mopping and cleaning my floors. The app is great since it shows you a map of where the robot went, and it’ll also show you a little itinerary of which rooms it’s doing in what order. However, setup and any resetting you need to do is a long process, so be ready to commit and troubleshoot when you unbox it. My long-term tester has also reported that its mopping abilities have not improved over the six months it's been running in her house, but it does best with vacuuming and carpet.

iRobot Roomba Max 875 Combo With ThermaMist for $799: As Roomba’s new top-line robot vacuum and mop, this model features 35,000 Pa of suction, as well as hot steam to pretreat stuck-on stains. However, what really sold me was the “no pre-clean pickup” advertised on the box. I’ve got pet toys, my teen’s sports equipment and shoes all over the floor, cords, and loose rugs; other robot vacuums I’ve tried have struggled with my household. The Max 875, however, moved through my house with ease—in fact, I was quite impressed with how well it powered through even the toughest robovac challenges, like shoelaces and a maze of tucked-in chairs around a table. It did fine on pedestrian stains on my LVP floors, like spilled coffee, but even with the ThermaMist and repeated returns to the scene, the 875 Combo couldn’t fully clean an area with dried wet cat food. Setup was also pretty buggy—I followed the manual, but the vacuum took off before I could add it to the app and map my house, trying to clean a random area on 14 percent battery life. It would then return to the dock station, charge for five minutes, and repeat this process for well over an hour. When I did get it connected to the app, it said it needed an update but was unable to download it. I eventually got it to work by factory-resetting the machine and starting all over, but this process took more patience than I’d expect at this price point. —Kat Merck

iRobot Roomba Plus 678 Combo Robot + AutoWash Dock for $599: Like its fancier sibling, the Max 875 above, the Plus 678 had a bit of a buggy setup process that required several attempts and a factory reset. The Plus 678 also has the Max 875’s AI-powered stain pretreatment (though without the ThermaMist steam) and 30,000 Pa of suction for Roomba’s new “SealForce” technology, which lowers a skirt around carpets to suction deeper into the pile. I tested this with three different types of rugs—a regular-pile wool rug, a loose washable rug, and a low-pile faux fur rug. It did well on the first two, but failed on the third, becoming fully stuck. (Most vacuums can’t handle this rug, so I don’t exactly fault it for this.) Other than the setup mishaps—which included false “brush roller failure” messages and a mapping attempt that left it turning around in circles in the middle of an open room for 20 minutes—this is a serviceable mop-vac with a feature list that’s hard to fault at this price. —Kat Merck

iRobot Roomba Plus 575 Combo Robot + AutoWash Dock for $499: After hearing about the futuristic Roomba growing up, I was excited to see one in action. During setup, I found that the battery cover unscrewed, but assumed it was intentional since no screws were included. It soon fell off, so I taped it; days later, it came off during cleaning and got lost, leaving the battery and cords exposed to debris and the wet mop. Not great. From the start, it struggled to map my home. Cleaning requires app routines, which I didn’t love, as sometimes I just wanted to be able to click a single room and go without having to create another routine. The routines were often ignored or stopped midway. A mop pad fell off on every single run, forcing me to retrace the machine’s path to find it in my home. It also got caught on cords and repeatedly tried to climb my cat tree’s base, getting stuck perpetually spinning until I had to manually move it. Edge cleaning was nonexistent; there was so much cat hair and dust near where the floor met the wall. After a month, it threw up and scattered debris whenever it crossed the ¾-inch thresholds to the bathroom, kitchen, and bedroom, so afterward I had to vacuum the mess it created—defeating the purpose. —Molly Higgins

Mova P10 Pro Ultra Gen2 for $360: This robot vacuum was solid, and especially did a good job with cleaning corners (it got a 2 out of 3 on the corner test, capturing both the stool and fridge Cheerios), but it did a poor job scrubbing away the cherry juice for my stain tests. One of the two stains was almost entirely left behind, and overall on casual runs of the vacuum it didn’t feel as if my floors were super clean. Still, if you’re looking for good corner cleaning, and carpets more than hard-floor deep cleaning, this is a solid robot vacuum for the price.

Roborock Saros 20 for $990: WIRED reviewer Adrienne So was mostly happy with this robot vacuum, as was I. She noticed the super-high suction (it hits 36,000 Pa) actually caused more debris to be left behind on her hard floors when it passed over thresholds; I didn't have this issue with the thresholds in my home, but instead I found debris on my hard floors immediately after having this vacuum clean them, with no threshold required. It also only got a one out of three in my Cheerio test, which isn't great for such an expensive vacuum.

Tapo RV50 Pro Omni for $400: After testing several robovacs that made me want to chuck them out the window, I had high hopes for Tapo’s new model that was released this summer. It promised over four hours of run time, dual-laser obstacle avoidance, DeepEdge mopping for corners and edges, and automatic floor detection to keep mops off carpets. But during more than two weeks of testing, it never mapped my home correctly or fully cleaned it. It couldn’t cross the ¾-inch raised thresholds into my kitchen or bathroom, and it mapped my bedroom but detected a phantom obstacle and cleaned only the 2-foot entryway. My kitchen, bathroom, and bedroom were never fully cleaned during testing. It’d be heading for the dock to wash mops or empty them and would forget to do the hall next or finish the living room and begin charging again. About half the time, the app asked me to map my home again, apparently forgetting the previous day’s map. During mapping, it sometimes started cleaning, got lost, and then announced it couldn’t find its dock, leaving me to locate and return it. When vacuuming, it sometimes left the mops at the station, returned for them, forgot, and began charging, thus ending its task. Not once did it successfully vacuum and mop my whole home. Online reviews are glowing, so perhaps I got a dud—but this experience was enough to make me want to clean by hand instead. —Molly Higgins

I test all robot vacuums in my three-story townhouse, where they clean across luxury vinyl plank (LVP); tile; carpet; and a large, low-pile rug. I have a dining table and four barstools to navigate, and both a cat and a child who create daily messes. I run the vacuum at least three times across the main floors of my home to assess its overall performance and note any recurring issues or errors it encounters. I do pick up my son’s toys, but I like to watch how the robot navigates the various chair legs and side tables throughout my home, and whether it sucks up the power cords beside my bed. I also like to see how much battery life is left after a run is complete on each level of my home.

My corner test, using three Cheerios in three corner (or cornerlike) spots.

I also set up an obstacle course of sorts. The first one is the corner test, created by three Cheerios placed in three tricky corners on the middle floor of my home: one in the corner of an Ikea Billy bookshelf toe kick, one underneath my countertops next to the fridge, and one next to a barstool chair leg. It’s how I test how well each robot vacuum gets into corners and underneath cabinetry.

My spill test, with two spots of cherry juice on the floor.

I also create intentional spills for these vacuums to clean up. I use maraschino cherry juice to create two spill spots, then use a paper towel to smear and thin the stain to better replicate a spill you might not have seen on your floors. Many robot vacuums have AI that promises to detect these kinds of stains, but so far, no vacuum has stopped and scrubbed both spots on its first try.

Can You Use Robot Vacuums on All Kinds of Floors?

You can, especially since there are so many mopping models now to better clean hard flooring. You can use these devices on anything from hardwood to LVP and tile, though I wouldn't recommend leaving smaller rugs out for these autonomous gadgets to get stuck on. Large, set rugs are fine, but bathroom and kitchen mats or any thin, easily moved rugs should be cleared out of the way and put in the wash instead of vacuumed by your robot vac.

How Often Do You Need to Maintain Your Robot Vacuum?

Taking good care of your robot vacuum will help it last. Here’s the debris-removal process you should follow for each robot vacuum style.

Make sure to review your robot vacuum’s manual for any other steps the manufacturer recommends you take regularly to keep the vacuum running for as long as possible. Many brands also have replacement parts, so you can swap out individual pieces like brushes without needing an entirely new vacuum.

Do I Still Need a Regular Vacuum if I Have a Robot Vacuum?

I recommend keeping some kind of vacuum on hand, though that can vary based on your home. If you have stairs, you’ll definitely still want a hand vacuum or stick vacuum that can easily maneuver and clean your staircase, while pet owners might want a vacuum that can clean upholstery. I prefer my Dyson stick vacuums for a good carpet clean, but your mileage may vary depending on your preferences. Either way, I think everyone needs a companion vacuum of some kind with a robot vacuum.

You don’t need it, but a self-emptying dock makes using a robot vacuum much easier. You aren’t fumbling with debris every time it runs, and having a single bag to remove or a bin to empty is much easier than pulling debris out of the vacuum itself. I’d even recommend choosing a stick vac with a self-emptying dock, as it just makes the whole experience so much easier.

How Does WIRED Obtain Robot Vacuums? What Happens When We’re Done Testing?

Almost all the robot vacuums we test are provided to us as press samples with the understanding that there is no guarantee of coverage or type of coverage. Most companies don’t want a used vacuum back, so we either donate them locally or have the top performers long-term tested to see how they last.

#271. Half of NASA's aging Mars fleet knocked offline by technical issues

Perseverance is having trouble transmitting to Earth. Odyssey is rapidly burning through its waning fuel supply.

Two of NASA’s four missions operating at Mars have suspended science operations after encountering separate technical issues in recent weeks.

The missions affected by the outages—hopefully temporary—are NASA’s Perseverance rover and Odyssey orbiter. Both are operating beyond their original design lifetimes. Perseverance is in its sixth year exploring the surface of Mars, having collected rock and soil samples for eventual return to Earth. The rover is now studying the rim of a crater that once contained an ancient lake of liquid water. Odyssey arrived in orbit around Mars in 2001 and is the longest-lived Mars mission in history.

The problem on Perseverance stems from the rover’s communications system. The rover has two redundant UHF radios for high-rate communications with a fleet of orbiters that relay data to Earth. A separate X-band system is available for direct-to-Earth communications at a lower data rate.

One of the rover’s two UHF radios was unresponsive when it powered up on October 30, triggering an automatic switch to the backup radio and placing the rover in safe mode. Ground teams at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California later discovered the backup UHF radio was transmitting at about half of its expected power output, NASA said in a statement last week.

“The team has stopped using both radios until they can evaluate potential causes of the issues and one or both are deemed safe to resume operating,” NASA said.

Perseverance is now transmitting signals directly to Earth in X-band, but the connection provides a “significantly lower data rate” than relaying signals through orbiters using the UHF radios. Mission managers paused the rover’s science operations “out of an abundance of caution” as they investigate the radio problem. Their initial focus is on getting the backup UHF radio running before turning their attention to recovering the primary radio, NASA said.

“The team is hopeful the rover could return to science by the end of November.”

The six-wheeled robot broke a record last month for the farthest any vehicle has driven on another planet. The Perseverance rover surpassed the 28.06-mile (45.16-kilometer) mark set by NASA’s Opportunity rover, which stopped working in 2018. Perseverance’s odometer now sits at twice the rover’s original goal for distance traveled.

The situation with the Odyssey orbiter seems more dire. One of the four reaction wheels used for pointing the spacecraft stopped spinning in early November, leaving Odyssey with two good wheels after the first one failed in 2013. The orbiter needs at least three wheels to keep it oriented correctly.

“Without the three reaction wheels, the spacecraft must rely solely on its hydrazine thrusters to remain oriented,” NASA said. The orbiter requires stable pointing to turn its solar arrays toward the Sun and its science instruments toward Mars.

Odyssey was running low on propellant before the reaction wheel malfunction, but managers were optimistic that with “extremely low” fuel usage, the orbiter would have enough to continue operating through at least the end of 2028, said Jeffrey Plaut, Odyssey’s project scientist at JPL, in a presentation earlier this year.

That assumed no failures in Odyssey’s three remaining reaction wheels. Without three healthy wheels, engineers estimate the spacecraft has enough hydrazine fuel to last one to two months, NASA said. The good news is that ground teams had some initial success troubleshooting the balky reaction wheel. Further testing is necessary to determine whether the wheel is recoverable.

Odyssey is one of four orbiters NASA uses to relay data between Earth and the Perseverance and Curiosity rovers on the Martian surface. Curiosity is still driving and collecting data after 14 years on Mars. The other three relay craft are NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, which reached the red planet in 2006, the European Space Agency’s 10-year-old ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter, and ESA’s 23-year-old Mars Express spacecraft.

NASA lost contact with its MAVEN orbiter last December after 11 years of operations at Mars when the spacecraft suddenly spun out of control. An investigation could not identify a specific root cause, but engineers concluded that a radiation-induced single event upset or a software issue caused MAVEN’s flight computer to reboot, according to Tiffany Morgan, director of NASA’s robotic Mars Exploration Program.

MAVEN’s inertial measurement unit failed to provide the computer with correct information on the spacecraft’s orientation, causing it to spin in response to the faulty data, Morgan said in a November 9 presentation to the Mars Exploration Program Analysis Group.

NASA is preparing to send reinforcements to renew the agency’s presence at Mars. In September, NASA awarded Blue Origin a $700 million contract for the Mars Telecommunications Network (MTN), an orbiter dedicated to providing high-bandwidth connectivity between Earth and other missions operating on and around the red planet.

NASA wanted Blue Origin to complete the telecom orbiter by the end of 2028 and have it operational at Mars in 2030. But the Mars Telecommunications Network is on hold after Rocket Lab, which lost its bid to win the MTN contract, filed a protest with the Government Accountability Office. The GAO is expected to rule on the protest next month, at which time Blue Origin could start work on the NASA contract if the government rejects Rocket Lab’s petition.

Another Mars mission, SkyFall, could also launch in 2028. NASA aims to send three helicopter drones to Mars to explore the planet’s geology and weather from the air.

A perennial priority for Mars scientists is replacing the unique high-resolution mapping camera on the aging Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter. Such a capability will help identify landing sites for future robotic and human missions, including a potential mission to return Perseverance’s rock specimens to Earth.

NASA is in the very early stages of developing a mission concept that could take over MRO’s imaging capability, but there’s no firm schedule or budget for such an undertaking. NASA will likely rely on MRO for landing-site reconnaissance well into the 2030s.

With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.
